2D PINN Inpainting — A Guided Tutorial (marimo, slim edition)

Reconstructing a CFD velocity field from a handful of sensors

This is the slim marimo version of notebooks/00_inpainting_complete.py. All the plotting and data-loading plumbing lives in the companion file pinn_utils_2d.py (same folder). Only the code that is the PINN method — the network, the autograd continuity residual, the loss, and the two training loops — stays visible here.

The problem

We have a steady CFD simulation of flow through a baffled contact basin (water winding around a set of baffles). Pretend we only measured the velocity at K scattered "sensor" points, far fewer than the thousands of mesh cells. Can we reconstruct the whole field?
  1. Baseline — a plain MLP. Fit the K sensors by regression. It nails the sensors and produces garbage in the gaps.
  2. The PINN. Same network, same sensors, but we also penalize violations of the incompressible continuity equation ||(\nabla\!\cdot\mathbf{u}=0||) at thousands of interior collocation points. That one physical law couples ||(U_x||) and ||(U_y||) everywhere, so a measurement in one place constrains the field elsewhere — and the gaps fill in.
This is the classic Raissi-style PINN inpainting setup, applied to a 2D turbulent flow.
marimo is reactive: move a slider and every dependent cell re-runs — no "Run All". Because training is slow, each model sits behind a ▶ Train button, so the notebook opens instantly. Cheap things (picking sensors, the "before" picture) update live as you drag sliders. Two files travel together: this notebook does from pinn_utils_2d import ..., so keep pinn_utils_2d.py in the same folder.

A quick glossary

Symbol / term Plain meaning
||((x, y)||) position in the basin
||(\mathbf{u}=(U_x, U_y)||) the velocity we want to reconstruct everywhere
sensor one of the ||(K||) mesh points whose velocity we pretend to have measured
held-out points every other mesh point — the network never sees these; we grade on them
collocation points scattered interior ||((x,y)||) where we check the physics, not the data
continuity ||(\partial U_x/\partial x + \partial U_y/\partial y = 0||) — mass conservation for incompressible flow
residual how badly a guess violates the equation (zero = perfect)
loss one number measuring "how wrong we are"; training pushes it toward 0
autograd PyTorch's automatic differentiation — exact derivatives of the network

Step 0 — Setup

We load the libraries and pull the shared plumbing from pinn_utils_2d.py: the CFD data loader and every plotting helper. We set the matplotlib backend to Agg (static images) before importing the helpers, so figures render cleanly inside marimo.

Step 1 — Load the CFD case

One CSV per case: each row is a mesh point with its ||((x, y, U_x, U_y)||). We normalize coordinates to ||([0,1]^2||) (via ||(x/L||), ||(y/W||)) and velocities by the inlet speed, so the network's inputs and outputs are all ||(O(1)||) — which keeps the autograd through the continuity residual numerically stable. CASE_ID = 834 is the 4-baffle case (the default). 267 is a simpler 1-baffle geometry.

Step 2 — Pick the sensors (live)

Choose how many sensors ||(K||) we get, and which random draw (seed) places them. Everything else — the whole basin — is held out: the network never sees it during training, and reconstruction error on those held-out points is the only score that matters. Drag the sliders and the picture below redraws instantly. Notice how little the network has to work with in the middle of the basin.

Step 3 — The network and the continuity residual

The pieces that are the PINN method stay visible below.
  • The network is a plain MLP mapping ||((x, y) \to (U_x, U_y)||): two inputs, tanh hidden layers, two outputs.
  • Why tanh and not ReLU? The physics loss needs the network's derivative, and that derivative must itself be differentiable (autograd differentiates the output w.r.t. the inputs). ReLU's second derivative is zero almost everywhere — useless for physics. tanh is smooth at every order.
  • The continuity residual. The network outputs live in normalized units, so the chain rule puts the ||(1/L||) and ||(1/W||) factors back: ||(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{u} = \tfrac{1}{L}\,\partial U_x/\partial x_\text{norm} + \tfrac{1}{W}\,\partial U_y/\partial y_\text{norm}||) create_graph=True is what lets gradients later flow back through this derivative to the weights.

Step 4 — Train the plain MLP (data only, no physics)

Standard supervised regression: the only loss is the mismatch between the network and the true velocity at the ||(K||) sensor locations. Every VAL_EVERY epochs we score the held-out points and keep the best checkpoint. Set the epoch budget and click Train. The reconstruction panels below grade each model with the pointwise L2 vector error ||(\;e(\mathbf{x}) = \lVert \mathbf{u}_\text{pred}(\mathbf{x})-\mathbf{u}_\text{true}(\mathbf{x})\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\left(U_x^\text{pred}-U_x^\text{true}\right)^2 + \left(U_y^\text{pred}-U_y^\text{true}\right)^2}||). It penalizes a wrong direction as well as a wrong speed — unlike ||(\bigl|\,\lVert\mathbf{u}_\text{pred}\rVert-\lVert\mathbf{u}_\text{true}\rVert\,\bigr|||), which can look small even when the predicted vector points the wrong way.

Step 5 — Train the same network with continuity

Identical network, identical sensor data. The only additions:
  1. Collocation points — thousands of random interior ||((x, y)||) where we ask the network to satisfy ||(\nabla\!\cdot\mathbf{u}=0||). These are not observations. (Note: for simplicity they're drawn uniformly over the whole ||([0,1]^2||) bounding box — including inside the solid baffles, where there is no flow. Both the collocation loss and the divergence diagnostic below do this, so the MLP-vs-PINN comparison stays fair; masking the baffle regions is a natural refinement.)
  2. The loss becomes ||(\;L_\text{data} + \lambda\cdot\text{ramp}(ep)\cdot L_\text{continuity}||).
  3. A warmup ramp eases the physics weight in over the first fraction of training, so the data term can anchor the prediction before the physics starts pulling.
||(\lambda||) sets how hard the physics pulls. Try the default (1.0) first, then sweep it.

Step 6 — Head to head

Same network, same sensors — the only difference is that one obeyed one physical law. The six panels below show truth, both reconstructions, both error fields, and a per-point improvement map (blue where the PINN beats the MLP). The divergence panels confirm the PINN's field is genuinely physical, and the loss curves show the data and physics terms dropping together. Watch the title: at the sweet-spot ||(K\approx 50||) the PINN typically cuts held-out error by roughly a quarter to a third. Push ||(K||) very low (both fail) or very high (the MLP no longer needs help) and the gap shrinks — retrain after moving the sliders to see it.

Step 7 — Deeper comparison: where, how, and versus what baseline

A single held-out MSE hides where and what kind of error each model makes. Three sharper views (retrain both models above first, then these update):
  1. An RBF (radial-basis-function) interpolation baseline — a smooth surface built to pass through the ||(K||) sensor values by placing one radial "bump" per sensor and summing them: ||(\;f(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{j=1}^{K} w_j\,\varphi(\lVert \mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}_j\rVert)||), with a Gaussian kernel ||(\varphi(r)=e^{-(r/\varepsilon)^2}||). The weights ||(w_j||) are found by solving a small linear system so the surface matches every sensor exactly, and the width ||(\varepsilon||) is set from the typical sensor spacing. It is mesh-free and needs no network training and no physics — we simply interpolate ||(U_x||) and ||(U_y||) separately. This is the honest "why not just interpolate the sensors?" baseline the network has to beat.
  2. Error vs. distance to the nearest sensor — turns "the PINN wins in the gaps" into a curve.
  3. Angular-error distribution — how far each field points in the wrong direction (magnitude alone can look fine while the vector is wrong), as a magnitude-weighted histogram of MLP vs PINN. A leftward shift of the PINN curve means it points the right way more often.

Step 8 — Adding turbulent momentum (RANS k-ε closure)

Continuity couples ||(U_x||) and ||(U_y||), but it is only one equation. The next rung on the completeness ladder is the momentum balance. For this turbulent basin the relevant form is the steady, incompressible RANS momentum equation with a Boussinesq eddy-viscosity closure: ||[(\mathbf{u}\cdot\nabla)\mathbf{u} = -\nabla P^{*} + \nabla\!\cdot\!\big[(\nu+\nu_t)(\nabla\mathbf{u}+\nabla\mathbf{u}^{\top})\big].||]Three things this needs that continuity did not:
  1. Pressure. Momentum contains ||(\nabla P||), and we have no pressure sensors — so we add a third network output ||(p||) and let it be inferred from momentum consistency (it is fixed only up to a constant). That output is the modified pressure ||(P^{*}=p/\rho+\tfrac{2}{3}k||); the ||(\tfrac{2}{3}k||) piece is negligible here.
  2. Second derivatives. The viscous term is a Laplacian, so the residual needs ||(\partial^2\mathbf{u}||) — a second autograd pass (another reason for the smooth tanh).
  3. The turbulence, supplied — not solved. We do not solve the ||(k||) and ||(\varepsilon||) transport equations. Instead we supply the eddy viscosity ||(\nu_t(x,y)||) the CFD already computed and use ||(\nu_{\text{eff}}=\nu+\nu_t||). That is the honest move for this dataset: the median ||(\nu_t||) is ~16,000× the molecular ||(\nu||), so a molecular-only ("laminar") momentum law would be badly wrong — turbulence carries essentially all the momentum transport. (We also freeze ||(\nu_t||) locally, i.e. neglect ||(\nabla\nu_t||), so the viscous term stays a clean ||(\nu_{\text{eff}}\nabla^2\mathbf{u}||).)
The loss becomes ||(\;L_\text{data} + \lambda_c\,L_\text{continuity} + \lambda_m\,L_\text{momentum}||), each physics term eased in with the same warmup ramp. Momentum is a partial extra constraint, so expect a modest further gain over continuity — and a striking bonus: a pressure field the network reconstructs without ever seeing one.

Per-term loss trajectories (RANS-momentum PINN)

Same read as the continuity-only curves, now with the momentum term. Watch the held-out val (green) and its distance to the data loss (blue) — the generalization gap. If the extra physics is helping the network generalize, this gap should be no worse — ideally tighter — than the continuity-only run in Step 6.

Wrapping up — what to take away

  • The loss is the physics. The PINN and the MLP differ by exactly one term — a squared continuity residual at collocation points — yet the PINN reconstructs the gaps the MLP cannot, because that one law couples ||(U_x||) and ||(U_y||) across the whole domain.
  • Derivatives come for free from autograd — that is what makes "obey the equation" measurable, and why we need a smooth activation like tanh.
  • Physics buys data efficiency in the sparse regime. The win is largest around ||(K\approx 50||). It is not magic at every scale — see below.
  • More physics is a ladder, not a switch. Step 8 adds the RANS ||(k\text{-}\varepsilon||) momentum balance (with the eddy viscosity supplied from the CFD) on top of continuity. It is a partial extra constraint, so it buys a further, smaller gain — and, as a bonus, the network reconstructs a pressure field it was never shown. Completeness (continuity → momentum → closure) is what steadily tightens the generalization gap.
Things to try (move sliders, then retrain):
  1. Sensor sparsity. Set ||(K=20||) then ||(K=300||) and retrain both models. At low ||(K||) both fail; at high ||(K||) the MLP interpolates fine on its own and the gap collapses — sometimes continuity even slightly hurts. That is incomplete physics meeting sufficient data, and it is a feature to teach.
  2. The physics weight ||(\lambda||). Sweep it ||(\{0, 0.25, 1, 3, 5\}||). Is bigger always better? (Watch the data loss in the curves — too much ||(\lambda||) and physics fights the data anchor.)
  3. Seed variance. Hold ||(K=50||) and step the seed 42 to 46, retraining each time. The improvement swings ~2x across which points you happen to sense — always report a range, never one lucky number.
  4. A different case. Set CASE_ID = 267 in Step 1 (simpler 1-baffle flow). The sweet spot moves to a lower ||(K||).
  5. The momentum weight ||(\lambda_m||) (Step 8). Sweep it and watch the RANS loss trajectories: does adding momentum lower the held-out val and tighten the generalization gap, or just trade data fit for physics? Compare its gap with the continuity-only run.
Where the plumbing lives: all data-loading and plotting code is in pinn_utils_2d.py, documented with docstrings. The plot_* helpers return their Figure, which is why the cells above wrap them in mo.as_html(...). Reference. Raissi, M., Perdikaris, P., & Karniadakis, G. E. (2019). Physics-informed neural networks. Journal of Computational Physics, 378, 686-707. doi:10.1016/j.jcp.2018.10.045
